newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Commodity markets see new price hikes on coffee.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Commodity markets see new price hikes on coffee.

text.p: World coffee prices extended a powerful rally on Wednesday and another big roaster, this time in the Netherlands, passed on the rising cost of beans to the supermarket shelf.

Elsewhere in the commodity markets prices were mostly rangebound, although aluminium showed a late gain. German economic research group IFO forecast steady global commodity prices over the medium term.
London futures for robusta coffee beans hit a six-week high of $1,766 per tonne for the July contract. The last time it graced those levels was on March 11 when it closed at $1,760.
The increase in raw coffee prices filtered through to more heavyweight wholesalers as Dutch roasters Douwe Egberts, which holds 70 percent of the local market, announced they were raising prices.
It was the third Dutch increase this year and followed retail price hikes in the United States and Germany.
Futures prices for robusta beans, mostly used in making soluble or instant coffee, have risen by one-third since the start of 1997 while arabica types, traded in New York, have doubled.
But the benchmark New York arabica contract took a breather from its meteoric rise to sit at 212.75 cents per pound on Wednesday.
The rally on arabica coffee reignited last week on fears of tight Latin American supply and the onset of the Brazilian frost season.
The industry took some relief when a strike by truckers in the Columbian port of Cartegena stopped after just one day after failing to trigger nationwide labour action.
The IFO forecast said coffee prices, which shed 26 percent in 1996, would rise 31 percent in 1997 and be steady in 1998.
The rangebound trading across most other commodity markets coincided with the IFO saying that commodity prices generally would hold level this year and rise four percent in 1998.
IFO forecast wheat prices off 23 percent in 1997 and seven percent next year and maize off 19 and five percent.
On Wednesday, the benchmark Chicago Board of Trade July wheat contract firmed to hold its head above the four dollar per bushel mark at $4.06-1/2.

Wheat "spiked" up to a high of $4.59 on April 21 after floods and a cold snap in the United States and worries about a prolonged dry spell in western Europe. Weather concerns have somewhat abated in recent days. Rain has fallen in Europe.
Traders at the London Metal Exchange saw little movement in most industrial metals but aluminium jumped late in London's day to end the afternoon at a six-week high at $1,661, up $29 on the day.
Traders cited good demand for the metal, a fall in warehouse stocks and buying by speculative funds.
The price of palladium, a rare white metal, stood out after dropping on news Russia may have signed a long-awaited decree to resume exports halted since December.
In a knee-jerk reaction spot palladium slipped to $153.25 an ounce from a peak of $159.00, losing $2.50 on the day.
The metal, used in electronics and autocatalysts, had gained 42 percent since December as Russia, the world's top supplier, pulled out of the market due to apparent bureaucratic snags.
Gold held just above $340.00 an ounce, down from $344.00 seen on Tuesday.

Crude oil prices were somewhat firmer on good heating oil demand. Cold weather has hit Europe and the benchmark Brent Blend of North Sea crude for July traded as much as 15 cents up in London at $18.30 per barrel at one point.
IFO said energy prices would drop one percent in 1997 and a further five percent in 1998 after a 15 percent rise in 1996.
